must_carry.question: Why did the narrator and Mona hunt for their new apartment in Brooklyn Heights, and who alone was to learn the address?
must_carry.answer: They wanted to be as far as possible from everyone they knew, above all Kronski and Arthur Raymond, so their fresh start would be free of intrusions, and only Ulric was to be given the new address.

must_carry.question: After the ten-dollar deposit on the ninety-dollar Brooklyn Heights flat, how did Mona raise the rest of the first month's rent?
must_carry.answer: Set on moving in, she got the remaining eighty dollars from one of her admirers, a room clerk at the Broztell whose name the narrator had never heard before.

must_carry.question: What was happening to the narrator's job at the telegraph company during the happy first months in the new apartment?
must_carry.answer: Because he had lost all interest in the work and wanted only to start writing, he did less and less at the office, slipped off to films, galleries and dance halls on invented errands, and was off sick ever more often, so the job was heading for a collapse.

must_carry.question: What name does the narrator give the Brooklyn Heights apartment, and what reason does he offer for loving it so much?
must_carry.answer: He calls it their Japanese love nest for its bare, spotless simplicity, and suggests he loved it so because he already knew it could not last long.

must_carry.question: After a cantor's singing from a radio shop near the Scotch bakery brings Mona to tears, the narrator offers to become a Jew and marry her again before a rabbi; how does she answer?
must_carry.answer: She laughs, tells him she does not want him to become a Jew and does not want to be one herself, says she is simply a woman and nothing more, and begs him never to bring the subject up again.

must_carry.question: Reading the Book of Ruth in the worn Bible Crazy George left behind, what does the narrator reflect about Mona's name?
must_carry.answer: He reflects that Mona was once called Mara and that she has turned her back on her own people and on the name they gave her.

must_carry.question: What vow does the narrator make on the morning he walks out of his job at the telegraph company?
must_carry.answer: Freshly free and a few months short of thirty-three, he swears never again to work for anyone or take orders, but to develop his talent and become a writer even if he starves for it.

must_carry.question: Which old possession does the narrator long to get back on the day he quits, and who has it now?
must_carry.answer: His old racing bicycle, a special Chemnitz-built machine he bought from a German rider after a six-day race and sold about two years earlier to a cousin living nearby, who he hopes will sell it back.

must_carry.question: When the narrator comes home having quit, what does Mona tell him about writing and about money?
must_carry.answer: She says he needs a long rest before he even thinks of writing and that he must leave their living to her, because if she can support her idle family she can surely support the two of them.

must_carry.question: What becomes of the Coney Island article and the other pieces the narrator sends out to magazine editors?
must_carry.answer: Not one is accepted; week after week they travel from editor to editor and come back with standard rejection slips, yet he sticks to the writing programme pinned on his wall.

must_carry.question: What did the narrator's bluntest friends say about the difference between his talk and his writing?
must_carry.answer: They told him he was always himself when he talked but not when he wrote, so he should write the way he talks, advice he first thought absurd and insulting but which later proved fruitful.

must_carry.question: What happens to the narrator's weekly visits to Maude and their little daughter once he is no longer earning?
must_carry.answer: The partings are harrowing (once in the park the child's embrace left him sobbing), and he starts putting the visits off and sending the alimony by post or messenger, while Mona, who carries the burden of raising that money, urges him to go.

must_carry.question: According to the start of chapter 3, whose name will go on the work the narrator submits for publication after his first three published pieces, and what is agreed about his part?
must_carry.answer: Mona's name, with one odd exception; it is agreed that he can do nothing on his own and is simply to write and leave everything else to her.

must_carry.question: When O'Mara turns up after a Caribbean fishing voyage, during the couple's first money crisis, what does he do with his earnings?
must_carry.answer: He empties his pockets onto the table as a shared fund for the household, a few hundred dollars, enough to clear their debts or to live on for a month or two.

must_carry.question: When Osiecki, the architect who finds lice in his desk every morning, drops in late at night, what does he leave untold?
must_carry.answer: He says he would rather get the matter of his girl off his chest, then stops, says it is getting late, and promises to tell them another time.

must_carry.question: What does the magazine man McFarland ask of the narrator after hearing him describe his years at the telegraph company?
must_carry.answer: He tells him to go home and start that night on a serial for the first issue of his new magazine, told plainly just as he had narrated it aloud rather than in a literary style, and promises more exciting assignments, even abroad, if it goes well.

must_carry.question: Why is Mona weeping on the evening the narrator returns from his meeting with McFarland?
must_carry.answer: She had visited her mother and learned that a mortgage on the family house must be paid at once or the house will be lost, and, worse for her, her mother treated her with contempt, refused to believe she was married and called her a whore.

must_carry.question: At MacGregor's dinner in Flatbush, how does the narrator respond to McFarland's serial offer and to the jobs MacGregor and O'Mara have lined up for him?
must_carry.answer: He says he is not ready for, or does not want, that kind of success and admits he does not yet know how to write, and he refuses any job at all, publicity, newspaper or otherwise, wanting only to go his own way.
